I'm wondering if this cartridge design would result in a bit of a loss of accuracy, since the round is fully encased in plastic and doesn't start out already in the bore of the barrel, this might cause a bit of variation in velocity. This might not matter much at the ranges modern infantry carbines are designed for, but CT-design rounds may not be suitable for sniping.

Edit: Link to original PDF

130 gr 7.62 NATO seems so weird - I almost called bullshit. I don't shoot my M1A with anything less than 165 gr. But I guess I use mine more as a marksman than as a rifleman*. Though if you're shooting stuff that light, an intermediate cartridge loses a lot of its disadvantages.

They've been looking at a 6.5 Grendel for years now and it's only made minor inroads. Guess the developers aren't taking the top brass to the right country clubs. The real innovation here is the cartridge telescoping polymer case. It LOOKS like it would seal well enough around the bullet until the bullet has entered the barrel and formed to the rifling. It also looks like there is zero free room in the case for extra powder, so the ballistics you see are as flat as they're going to get. Then again they may have determined that the required ogive starts to lose stability somewhere near that velocity (discussed in the article you posted). At any rate, replacing the brass with polymer (which looks to be even more by volume, though lots less by mass) seems to eliminate 30-35% of the weight of the cartridge, one of the main factors in infantry not regularly carrying a battle rifle. I have to wonder how much more stress this puts on the chamber - brass isn't that firm (which is why it's used - it seals to the breech), but I have to think that polymer just isn't as strong.

Any way, there's lots of neat stuff to consider related to CT rounds, especially the 6.5 Grendel CT and what you might be able to do (and what you might have to do) with a 7.62x51 CT.

* Note I'm not nor have never been military, so factor that in when considering my opinion. Selection of gear carried by the military should generally be up to the military, and not civvies who have never been under fire.

I don't think brass contributes much to strength at all, that's the chamber's job. It'd be more important around the base, so the chamber would need to be more fully supported or the base of the round would be mostly plastic.
